power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: From Behavioral Design to Behavior-Based Design: Functional Specification for Designed Environments

text.text: Behavioral design has developed frameworks and taxonomies that help researchers and practitioners organize, select, and describe interventions.
However, identifying an intervention technique does not establish the functional relations through which it influences behavior.
This article proposes behavior-based design (BBD) as a programmatic approach that places functional specification at the center of the design process.
BBD does not introduce new behavioral principles or replace established methods of behavior analysis.
Instead, it organizes their application to deliberately designed environments, including digital interfaces, public services, sustainability initiatives, and organizational systems.

The article identifies five criteria for adequate functional specification: behavioral precision, functional coherence, discriminability among alternative functional explanations, relevance to design decisions, and empirical accountability.
Examples illustrate how the same intervention category may involve different functional relations, leading to different predictions, measurement strategies, and design decisions.
Particular attention is given to competing contingencies, maintenance, generalization, and the conditions affecting those responsible for implementing and sustaining interventions.
Finally, the article outlines a research agenda for comparing designs informed by explicit functional hypotheses with approaches relying primarily on broader intervention categories.

The proposed contribution of BBD is therefore methodological and programmatic: to make 2 functional specification an explicit requirement of design and to evaluate its predictive and practical value through cumulative empirical research.
Behavior change has become a mainstream design problem.

Across policy, health, organizational practice, sustainability, public services, and digital systems, practitioners increasingly treat behavior as something to be arranged, measured, and modified rather than merely encouraged.
This development should be welcomed: it has legitimized behavioral outcomes, improved the reporting of intervention components, and moved many applied fields beyond intuition and common sense.
Digital product design shows the same shift.

Recent work on evidence-based digital design argues that the field has too often relied on personal experience, common sense, or isolated experiments and needs a stronger framework for predicting and influencing users' behavior (León Domínguez, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work on evidence-based digital design argues that the field has too often relied on personal experience, common sense, or isolated experiments and needs a stronger framework for predicting and influencing users' behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(León Domínguez, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this article, behavioral design is used broadly to refer to approaches that intentionally configure environments, interfaces, or services to influence behavior.
It is not treated as a single, unified discipline.

Much of this expansion has been driven by behavioral economics and related traditions, including nudging, choice architecture, and accounts of judgment and decision-making (Kahneman, 2011; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
text.formatted: Much of this expansion has been driven by behavioral economics and related traditions, including nudging, choice architecture, and accounts of judgment and decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kahneman, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Thaler & Sunstein, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: In parallel, structured frameworks such as the capability-opportunity-motivation-behavior model (COM-B), the Behavior Change Wheel, and the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy have given practitioners a shared vocabulary for designing, classifying, and reporting interventions (Michie et al., 2011 (Michie et al., , 2013)).
text.formatted: In parallel, structured frameworks such as the capability-opportunity-motivation-behavior model (COM-B), the Behavior Change Wheel, and the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy have given practitioners a shared vocabulary for designing, classifying, and reporting interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Michie et al., 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Michie et al., , 2013))</ref>.

text.text: These tools support interdisciplinary communication and make behaviorchange methods more accessible across fields.
These achievements matter: a field that once did not talk about behavior in systematic ways now often does.
Yet greater classificatory precision has not necessarily produced greater functional precision, and a shared vocabulary should not be mistaken for a shared explanatory system.
Taxonomies organize intervention labels.
They do not by themselves specify the functional relations through which behavior is selected, maintained, weakened, generalized, or replaced.

A design may be accurately classified as prompting, feedback, incentivization, environmental restructuring, or friction reduction while leaving open important questions about which behavior is affected, under what conditions, through which consequences, and for how long.
Whether a particular intervention is functionally underspecified remains an empirical and analytic question.
It cannot be inferred from its label alone.
Design itself has long recognized a similar problem.

Norman's critique of the loose use of "affordance" is instructive: designers often claimed to have "added an affordance" when they had actually added a visual cue, a convention, or feedback (Norman, 1999).
text.formatted: Norman's critique of the loose use of "affordance" is instructive: designers often claimed to have "added an affordance" when they had actually added a visual cue, a convention, or feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Norman, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: The same risk arises when an influence strategy or design feature is reported without specifying the behavioral function of the component.
The problem is not interdisciplinary terminology as such, but the tendency for useful terms to harden into labels that obscure the relations they were meant to clarify.
A common professional vocabulary may facilitate coordination while leaving functional integration incomplete.
Behavior analysis is well positioned to address this.

Its contribution is not merely a more technical vocabulary but an approach centered on the functional relations between behavior and environmental conditions, including response classes, antecedent and motivating variables, consequences, competing contingencies, and the conditions governing maintenance over time (Catania, 2017; Rasmussen et al., 2023; Skinner, 1953).
text.formatted: Its contribution is not merely a more technical vocabulary but an approach centered on the functional relations between behavior and environmental conditions, including response classes, antecedent and motivating variables, consequences, competing contingencies, and the conditions governing maintenance over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Catania, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Rasmussen et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Skinner, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: These are not ornaments attached to an otherwise complete intervention.
Specifying their relations is essential to understanding whether an intervention produces a transient effect, durable change, relapse, countercontrol, or no measurable change.
The argument also requires an internal critique.
Behavior analysis has achieved substantial applied impact, including instructional design, organizational behavior management, behavior-based safety, and environmental interventions.
These traditions establish that design problems are not foreign to the discipline.
Much of this work, however, has developed within specific applied domains.

For example, behavior-based safety has focused on workplace safety practices (Komaki et al., 1978; Sulzer-Azaroff, 1978), while organizational behavior management has examined performance feedback and organizational performance (Prue & Fairbank, 1981).
text.formatted: For example, behavior-based safety has focused on workplace safety practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Komaki et al., 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sulzer-Azaroff, 1978)</ref>, while organizational behavior management has examined performance feedback and organizational performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Prue & Fairbank, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Research on environmental interventions has similarly addressed specific problems such as energy conservation and recycling (Hayes & Cone, 1977; O'Connor et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Research on environmental interventions has similarly addressed specific problems such as energy conservation and recycling <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hayes & Cone, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">O'Connor et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These contributions provide an established foundation, but the literature considered here does not reveal a comparably recognizable, cumulative research program focused on the functional specification of designed environments across domains.
The extent to which existing behavior-analytic contributions already address this broader research objective remains to be systematically examined.
Behavior analysts already possess the relevant concepts.

What remains worth developing is a visible, cumulative, interdisciplinary program that organizes those concepts around the problems of deliberately designed environments and tests what functional specification adds to established design practice.
The primary audience of this article is therefore behavior analysts.
Its purpose is not to provide designers, policy researchers, sustainability researchers, or other professional communities with a complete behavior-analytic methodology in a single paper.
Those communities present different problems, vocabularies, constraints, and literatures.
Effective engagement will require domain-specific work in their own scholarly and professional venues.
The narrower task here is internal: to specify what behavior analysis can contribute to designed environments and how a research program around that contribution might begin.
The issue is therefore one of disciplinary participation as well as conceptual accuracy.

Without a coherent research program, behavior-analytic principles may continue to be cited indirectly, loosely interpreted, or rediscovered under new names, rather than systematically applied, evaluated, and examined for their ethical implications in the design of contemporary environments.
The article has two related goals.
First, it offers a behavior-analytic reappraisal of behavioral design by distinguishing taxonomic or process-level integration from functional specification.

Second, it proposes behavior-based design (BBD) as a programmatic research and design orientation through which behavior analysts can contribute more systematically to deliberately designed environments.
The term does not name a new theory, discipline, or replacement for behavioral design.
It names a focused invitation to bring established functional methods into interdisciplinary design research, while testing rather than assuming their added value.

The proposed orientation is analogous, in a limited programmatic sense, to behaviorbased safety: a recognizable effort to bring established behavior-analytic concepts and methods to problems in a defined applied arena, without founding a separate science.
The comparison should not conceal differences in maturity or evidence.
Behavior-based safety has a substantial applied history.
Behavior-based design, as used here, names a proposed interdisciplinary research program whose incremental contribution remains to be tested.

Functional and contingency analysis, organizational behavior management, and behavioral systems analysis already provide established approaches to analyzing existing environments and informing the design of new ones.
They are methodological antecedents, not competing approaches.

The proposed value of a separate programmatic designation lies in making functional specification an explicit and shared objective across applied design domains, systematically integrating it into the formulation of design problems, the selection of environmental arrangements, and the evaluation of their behavioral effects.
Whether this integration provides incremental predictive or practical value remains an empirical question.

Rather than replacing established behavior-analytic methods, BBD would organize their use around recurring design problems and support cumulative comparisons of how functional hypotheses influence design decisions, behavioral outcomes, maintenance, and generalization.

BBD is concerned with the broader design research problems of interfaces, artifacts, physical environments, services, and sociotechnical systems, rather than claiming exclusive jurisdiction over any of these domains.
Not all conceptual tools used in behavior change serve the same purpose.
Some organize practice, some describe intervention components, some propose general causal relations, and some specify the variables that make behavior more or less likely in a particular setting.
This distinction matters because coordination, classification, explanation, and functional analysis represent different levels of work.
Frameworks help teams map options and organize decisions.
Taxonomies provide consistent names for intervention components.
Process theories propose relations among variables.
Functional specification goes further by identifying the environmental and historical conditions under which a response class is likely to occur, persist, weaken, or generalize.

These levels are related but not interchangeable: a framework can be useful without being a process theory; a taxonomy can support reporting without explaining change; a process theory can suggest broad causal relations without specifying the contingencies at work in a given case.

Functional specification asks a more direct question: which relations among antecedents, response classes, consequences, motivating variables, histories, and competing contingencies account for the observed behavior?
COM-B and the Behavior Change Wheel are strong translational tools.

They link behavior to capability, opportunity, and motivation, and map these categories onto intervention functions such as education, restriction, and environmental restructuring (Michie et al., 2011).
text.formatted: They link behavior to capability, opportunity, and motivation, and map these categories onto intervention functions such as education, restriction, and environmental restructuring <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Michie et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy adds a more granular descriptive layer (Michie et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy adds a more granular descriptive layer <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Michie et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Their value is greatest for coordination and reporting, but their limitation appears when a category is treated as if it identified a behavioral process.

Recent research on behavioral design helps illustrate this distinction. Cash et al. (2017) examined 20 projects from one design firm and proposed a behavioral-design process, while Bay Brix Nielsen et al. (2021) synthesized cognition, ability, motivation, timing, and social and physical context into a "behavioral design space".
text.formatted: Recent research on behavioral design helps illustrate this distinction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cash et al. (2017)</ref> examined 20 projects from one design firm and proposed a behavioral-design process, while Bay Brix Nielsen et al. (2021) synthesized cognition, ability, motivation, timing, and social and physical context into a "behavioral design space".

text.text: These are meaningful contributions to design-process organization and the systematic exploration of design possibilities.
Yet the empirical assessment of process activities or the classification of design parameters is not, by itself, a functional analysis of the variables controlling a response class.
In Cash et al. (2017), project success also included perceived customer and team success and project-delivery indicators.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cash et al. (2017)</ref>, project success also included perceived customer and team success and project-delivery indicators.

text.text: Those outcomes should not be confused with demonstrations of behavioral mechanisms.

The authors do recommend experimentation, so the point is not that behavioral design excludes rigorous tests, but that design-process evaluation and functional identification answer distinct questions.
Likewise, broad dimensions such as motivation or physical context help designers explore options but can subsume different behavior-environment relations.
Bay Brix Nielsen et al. (2021) themselves acknowledge that their design-space framework does not yet capture interdependencies among its parameters.
A functional specification does not compete with these tools as a new taxonomy.

It asks which candidate relations are implicated, what observations might discriminate among them, and what different decisions would follow. Normand et al. (2021) reinforce this: many techniques cataloged in mainstream healthbehavior taxonomies overlap substantially with standard behavior-analytic procedures.
text.formatted: It asks which candidate relations are implicated, what observations might discriminate among them, and what different decisions would follow. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Normand et al. (2021)</ref> reinforce this: many techniques cataloged in mainstream healthbehavior taxonomies overlap substantially with standard behavior-analytic procedures.

text.text: The implication is not merely terminological.
Treated only as named components, these techniques leave their behavioral function underspecified.
The behavior-analytic contribution is to clarify when a component serves one of several distinct behavioral functions, for example as a discriminative stimulus or a response-effort manipulation.
Broad categories such as capability, opportunity, and motivation compress heterogeneous relations.

"Motivation," for instance, may refer to several distinct processes, including motivating operations, rule-governed behavior, reinforcement, avoidance, and competing consequences (Hackenberg, 2009; Malott, 1992; Michael, 1993; Odum, 2011), processes that are not interchangeable even when placed under one heading.
text.formatted: "Motivation," for instance, may refer to several distinct processes, including motivating operations, rule-governed behavior, reinforcement, avoidance, and competing consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hackenberg, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Malott, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Michael, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Odum, 2011)</ref>, processes that are not interchangeable even when placed under one heading.

text.text: Umbrella terms organize discussion but are too coarse to guide precise contingency design.
The same holds for common labels.
A prompt may act as a discriminative stimulus, a rule, or an inert reminder, depending on local reinforcement history.
Feedback may function as reinforcement, punishment, a discriminative stimulus, or mere information with no effect on responding.
An incentive may involve positive or negative reinforcement, conditioned reinforcement, delayed symbolic exchange, or rule-governed behavior.
The label says what the intervention resembles, not what it does.

Examples from human-computer interaction and ergonomics show why the distinction is practical. Chang et al. (2008) developed an interactive toothbrushing game with contingent audiovisual changes and direct behavioral measures, but the multicomponent evaluation does not isolate the reinforcing function of individual signals. Taverna et al. (2017) invoked positive reinforcement in the design of interactive hygiene products while evaluating primarily prototype comprehension and user experience. Brandenburg and Mirka (2005) found more favorable subjective responses to an ergonomic intervention with positive feedback but no comparable improvement in measured performance or discomfort.

text.text: Their findings are consistent with reinforcement hypotheses but do not directly establish the function of individual feedback events for individual users.
These studies pursue legitimate, different research objectives.
Their comparison suggests a constructive role for behavior analysts in designing tests that separate intervention effectiveness from claims about particular functional processes.
Existing frameworks have contributed to the organization and dissemination of behavioral interventions, but these contributions should not be confused with a functional account of behavior change.
Classifying an intervention as prompting, feedback, incentivization, or environmental restructuring does not explain why it works, under what conditions it works, or whether its effects will persist.
These questions require an analysis of the functional relations between behavior and environmental events.

Behavior-based design places this analysis at the center of the design process, making functional specification a fundamental requirement for developing, evaluating, and refining interventions rather than an optional addition to existing frameworks.

Applied behavior change literature often combines constructs from multiple traditions, from beliefs and intentions to habits, biases, engagement, and reinforcement, and presents this as comprehensiveness.
In practice it can become conceptual packaging: many terms are placed side by side without specifying the relations among them.
Invoked without independent operationalization, such constructs yield post hoc redescriptions of outcomes rather than functional accounts.
The relevant issue is what these labels leave unspecified, not whether every use of them is conceptually empty.
Terms such as motivation, engagement, friction, feedback, or incentive may summarize useful properties of an intervention.
The label alone, however, does not determine which behavioral process is operating.
This distinction can be demonstrated at the level of individual design problems.
This is not only a philosophical objection but a design problem.
Attributing a change to "motivation" still leaves the designer needing to know what to manipulate, under which conditions, and with what plan for consequences and maintenance.

When someone fails to complete an administrative form, attributing the failure to "low motivation" is less informative than examining the effort required, the clarity of the available cues, the delay of relevant consequences, and whether abandoning the task is reinforced by the immediate termination of aversive demands.
Consider a digital service that sends repeated reminders for an unfinished application while leaving response effort unchanged, the next step ambiguous, and the payoff delayed.
Whatever label is used, the functional question is whether the stimulus has acquired control over the relevant response class.

If completion is limited by high response effort or delayed consequences, or if abandonment is maintained by escape from aversive demands, repeated reminders may have little effect unless those conditions change.
The example also generates a prediction.
If failure to initiate the application is primarily related to weak stimulus control, a well-timed and discriminable reminder may increase initiation.

If abandonment is instead related to missing documents, repeated errors, high response effort, potentially reinforcing consequences of task termination, or stronger competing contingencies, increasing reminder frequency should have limited effects unless those conditions also change.
Classifying the intervention as "prompting" does not distinguish between these possible explanations, whereas functional specification can.
The alternatives imply different measurement plans.
Weak stimulus control suggests measuring initiation after discriminable cues and testing cue timing.
High response effort suggests recording step-level latencies, errors, attempts, and abandonment despite initiation.
Competing contingencies suggest observing allocations among the target task and alternative activities, where feasible.
The same overall completion rate can conceal these different patterns, so a category-based decision to send more reminders could miss the relevant variable.
These are discriminating hypotheses for future assessment, not functions established for a particular service.
Similarly, an organization may add a dashboard, described as feedback, to increase reporting.
Yet for the individual employee, accurate reporting may bring extra work, social friction, or blame, or have no visible effect at all.

Unless the dashboard changes the consequences of reporting, its stimulus control, its effort, or the value of competing responses, the intervention carries a behavioral label while the functional design stays weak.
Here, too, the difference is predictive rather than merely terminological.
If dashboard information functions as an effective consequence or discriminative stimulus, reporting should change in relation to its presentation.
If accurate reporting continues to produce extra work or blame, however, these consequences may discourage the very behavior the organization intends to promote.
The functional account therefore directs attention to the contingencies affecting reporting behavior, which the category "feedback" alone does not identify.
These examples illustrate why identifying an intervention technique is not sufficient to explain its effects.

Feedback, incentives, and environmental restructuring can influence behavior through different functional relations, depending on the conditions in which they are implemented and the individual's learning history (degli Espinosa & Hackenberg, 2024; Hackenberg, 2009).

text.text: Such descriptions may be useful, but they do not identify the variables responsible for the behavior observed.
A behavior-based approach requires designers to move beyond these categories and formulate testable hypotheses about the relations between behavior and environmental conditions.
The relevant question is not simply which technique to use, but which contingencies must be arranged, modified, or maintained to produce the intended behavioral outcomes.
Behavioral design often involves arranging antecedent conditions, such as prompts, defaults, and changes in the accessibility of available responses (Michie et al., 2011; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008).

text.text: These interventions can be useful, and antecedent control is an established part of behavior analysis (Catania, 2017; Rasmussen et al., 2023).

text.text: However, specifying antecedent arrangements alone is insufficient to explain how behavior is acquired and maintained.
A functional account must also consider the consequences of responding, relevant reinforcement histories, and competing contingencies.
A default may raise a target behavior by reducing effort or the immediate cost of an alternative.
A reminder can prompt a response when the repertoire exists and the cue has acquired function.
A dashboard may influence behavior when the information it presents acquires discriminative functions or participates in reinforcing or punishing contingencies.
But what happens in a different interface, routine, or context with stronger competing reinforcers?
Without a plan for maintenance and generalization, many interventions stay bounded to the engineered context (Stokes & Baer, 1977).
text.formatted: Without a plan for maintenance and generalization, many interventions stay bounded to the engineered context <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Stokes & Baer, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The problem may appear even before maintenance is tested: arranged consequences can be weak, delayed, or poorly connected to the target response.
An intervention may change the conditions under which a response occurs without establishing the contingencies needed to maintain that response over time.
A person may click, comply, attend, or complete a form once because the local arrangement makes that response temporarily easier.
Such one-time change should not be equated with a durable repertoire.
Behavior-based design is proposed here as an approach to the functional specification of deliberately designed environments.
It does not introduce new behavioral principles or distinguish a new science from behavior analysis.

Its proposed contribution is methodological and programmatic: it places functional specification at the center of the design process and organizes the application of established behavior-analytic methods to the development, evaluation, and refinement of designed environments.
Functional specification does not require a formal experimental functional analysis in every design project.
It requires an explicit, testable account of the response classes, antecedent conditions, consequences, competing contingencies, and maintenance variables judged relevant to the problem.

Its defining feature is therefore a change in the unit at which the design problem is represented: from intervention categories, psychological tendencies, or surface features to relations among contexts, response classes, consequences, histories, competing responses, and conditions of maintenance.
In complex designed environments, the analysis also includes the contingencies acting on the people and organizations that implement, maintain, and evaluate the design.

An adequate specification should identify the observable target and competing response classes, the antecedent and motivating conditions hypothesized to affect them, relevant consequences (including their timing and contingency), and plausible sources of competing reinforcement, avoidance, or response effort.

It should also describe expected conditions for maintenance and generalization, possible adverse effects or countercontrol, and, when relevant, the contingencies acting on designers, implementers, and organizations responsible for sustaining the arrangement.
An adequate functional specification does not require an exhaustive description of every variable that may influence behavior.
Its adequacy depends on the behavioral problem being addressed and the decisions that researchers and designers need to make.

At a minimum, it should identify the relevant response classes and competing alternatives, the antecedent and motivating conditions under which behavior occurs, and the consequences and competing contingencies hypothesized to influence responding.
Depending on the problem, it should also address maintenance, generalization, and the conditions required for successful implementation.

Five criteria are particularly important for evaluating the adequacy of functional specification: behavioral precision, functional coherence, discriminability among alternative functional explanations, relevance to design decisions, and empirical accountability.
Behavioral precision requires a clear definition of the responses under consideration.
Functional coherence requires an explicit account of how environmental conditions and consequences may influence those responses.
Discriminability concerns whether alternative functional explanations lead to different predictions or measurement strategies.
Relevance to design decisions requires that the analysis identify variables that can inform the selection or modification of an intervention.
Finally, empirical accountability requires that proposed functional relations remain open to observation, testing, and revision.
These criteria are not intended as a new checklist or validated assessment scale.
Rather, they establish standards for determining whether a functional account can meaningfully guide design.

Not every project requires an experimental functional analysis, but competing explanations should be sufficiently explicit to generate different predictions about behavior or suggest different intervention strategies.
It is also essential to distinguish between relations hypothesized on theoretical grounds, relations supported by observational evidence, and those demonstrated experimentally.
For example, providing a reward does not establish that it functions as a reinforcer, just as increased system use does not necessarily demonstrate a reinforcement process.

Functional specification is therefore adequate when it identifies the relevant behavioral relations, makes clear the evidence supporting them, and provides testable implications for design or evaluation.
Its contribution lies in what researchers and designers can predict, measure, manipulate, and revise on the basis of the analysis.
Simply describing familiar intervention techniques in behavior-analytic terminology does not meet this standard.
In designed environments, functional specification must also consider the contingencies affecting those responsible for implementing and maintaining an intervention.
An arrangement that supports the intended behavior of users may create additional effort, costs, or unfavorable consequences for managers, service providers, or other actors involved.
For example, a reporting procedure may improve accuracy while increasing a manager's workload, and a redesigned service may reduce user effort while increasing administrative costs.

These differences matter because the implementation and maintenance of an intervention depend not only on the contingencies affecting users, but also on those influencing the behavior of the people responsible for sustaining it.
Behavior-based design places these requirements at the center of the design process.

The relevant task is not simply to identify a suitable intervention category, but to specify the functional relations through which an intervention is expected to influence behavior and determine how those relations can be evaluated.
The same intervention label may correspond to different functional processes, with different implications for measurement, intervention selection, maintenance, and generalization.

text.text: It should be noted that the hypotheses are illustrative and do not establish the functions of intervention components.
Measures and comparisons are intended to distinguish plausible accounts, but additional experimental evidence may be needed to establish functional relations.
Public services, organizational systems, digital interfaces, and sustainability initiatives are all settings in which environmental conditions are deliberately arranged to influence behavior.
Access requirements, deadlines, prompts, feedback, and response costs can affect what people do, how often they respond, and whether their behavior persists.
However, the presence of these design features does not establish their behavioral function.
This is where functional specification becomes important.
Digital interfaces offer a particularly useful example because user responses can be measured and followed by programmed consequences (León Domínguez, 2025).
They provide opportunities to study how specific environmental arrangements influence behavior.

Behavior analysts have a mature science of many of these variables, and relevant applications already exist in organizational systems, instructional technologies, sustainability, and environmental design.
Yet these contributions have generally developed within bounded research traditions rather than under a shared, cross-domain program of functional specification for designed environments.
The issue is not that other fields necessarily ignore behavioral function, nor that a systematic census has established the absence of behavior analysts.
It is that their distinctive functional methods offer a concrete opportunity for more organized, cumulative participation in design research.
Several features may contribute to this limited visibility.

Behavior-analytic language can appear opaque to nonspecialists, the field's public identity is often narrowed to autism and special education despite a much broader tradition (Normand et al., 2021; Northup et al., 1993), and its methods may be perceived as better suited to controlled interventions than to complex, multilevel design problems.

text.text: The issue is strategic as well as scientific.
Designers already arrange environmental conditions that may influence behavior.
Interfaces present prompts, provide incentives, introduce delays, and restrict access.
Policies establish eligibility rules, deadlines, and penalties.
Organizations arrange performance measures and consequences.
The question is not whether behavior will be designed, but whether designed environments will be analyzed with rigor.
The following domains illustrate how functional specification can be applied.
They are not a representative sample from which the prevalence of functional underspecification can be estimated.
Their purpose is analytic: to show what additional questions become available when a design is represented in terms of response classes and contingencies rather than intervention labels alone.
The examples focus on sustainability, public services, and organizational systems.
Digital interfaces are considered throughout the article as designed environments that can also form part of these domains.

All three domains have generated behavior-analytic research or tools relevant to designed environments, and together they provide illustrative contexts in which a comparative research program could be developed (Gelino et al., 2021; León Domínguez, 2025; Normand et al., 2021; Prue & Fairbank, 1981; Sulzer-Azaroff, 1978).

Sustainability offers a clear case where the limits of merely classificatory design become visible.
Sustainable action is not one behavior.

Energy use, recycling, and transport choices involve different response classes (Gelino et al., 2021; Lange & Dewitte, 2019), each competing with alternatives that are cheaper, easier, or more immediately reinforcing.

Information alone has often proved weak, whereas feedback, incentives, and manipulations of response effort produce more reliable effects in energy-conservation research (Hayes & Cone, 1977 , 1981; Kohlenberg et al., 1976; Slavin et al., 1981; Staats et al., 2000; Van Houten et al., 1981; Winett et al., 1979 Winett et al., , 1982)).

text.text: The functional specification changes the question from "Does feedback work?"
or "Does reducing friction work?"
to questions about the conditions under which these arrangements alter responding.
For example, a feedback intervention should have different effects when information is immediate and response-contingent than when it is delayed and aggregated.
A friction manipulation should have different effects depending on the effort required by the target and competing responses.
These are testable differences hidden by the broad intervention label.
The lesson is not just that multicomponent interventions can work, but that effective design requires specifying target responses, competing reinforcers, effort, consequences, and maintenance.
A sustainability intervention, like any designed environment, should be analyzed by the contingencies it arranges, not the labels it carries.
Public services rely on behavioral chains, not isolated acts (Cooper et al., 2020; Moynihan et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Public services rely on behavioral chains, not isolated acts <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cooper et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Moynihan et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A user may have to detect a requirement, understand eligibility, gather documents, recover credentials, complete and upload forms, correct errors, attend appointments, make payments, and wait for delayed outcomes.
Administratively these register as single outcomes such as "application completed" or "appointment attended", but functionally they are extended chains under multiple sources of stimulus control.

Failure at any link gets labeled noncompliance or low motivation, even when the operative variables are response effort, ambiguous cues, weak or delayed consequences, punishment for errors, or stronger competing contingencies.
This matters especially in health and public-service settings, where important outcomes depend on what people do under specific environmental conditions.

Behavioral factors play an important role in public health (Schroeder, 2007), and Normand et al. (2021) identify several areas in which applied behavior analysis can contribute to public-health research and practice.
text.formatted: Behavioral factors play an important role in public health <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Schroeder, 2007)</ref>, and Normand et al. (2021) identify several areas in which applied behavior analysis can contribute to public-health research and practice.

text.text: Public administration presents different problems, but the need to specify the conditions influencing behavior is equally relevant.
A behavior-based analysis asks what the service requires the person to do, under what conditions, and with what consequences.

A reminder may function as a discriminative stimulus when the relevant response is in the repertoire and the stimulus signals conditions under which that response has previously contacted reinforcement.
The same reminder may have limited effects when the person lacks documents, cannot access the portal, expects error messages, or has competing obligations with more immediate payoffs.
The problem then is not a missing prompt but the arrangement of the whole contingency.
Consider benefit renewal, tax filing, or permit applications (Moynihan et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Consider benefit renewal, tax filing, or permit applications <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Moynihan et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The target is treated as "submitting the form", but functionally the task is a chain of smaller responses such as finding the portal, recalling a password, interpreting official language, retrieving documents, correcting errors, and confirming.
At some steps, abandoning the task may provide immediate relief from effortful or aversive demands, while the benefits of completing the procedure remain delayed or uncertain.
This example shows the practical difference between classification and functional specification.
A label-based account may identify "send reminder" or "reduce friction" as intervention components.
A functional account first identifies where the chain breaks.
If users reach the portal but stop at password recovery, a general reminder should have little effect relative to reducing effort at that link.
If users possess the required documents and skills but fail to initiate the chain, a discriminable reminder delivered under appropriate conditions may be sufficient.
If users complete the chain once but fail at the next renewal, the design problem shifts again from acquisition to maintenance.
The same top-level outcome, noncompletion, therefore implies different interventions depending on the controlling relations.
Missed healthcare appointments can be understood in the same way (Boksmati et al., 2016; Werner et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Missed healthcare appointments can be understood in the same way <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boksmati et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Werner et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than treating them simply as failures of engagement, it is more useful to analyze them as a sequence of required steps: booking the appointment, confirming it, arranging transport, arriving, and checking in.
Each step may involve different barriers, such as effort, waiting time, competing responsibilities, and benefits that occur only later.
In some cases, a text reminder may be enough.
In other cases, the main problem is not the lack of a reminder, but the effort required, competing demands, and delayed outcomes.

Behavior-based redesign would decompose the outcome into component responses, reduce effort, sharpen cues, confirm completed steps, preserve progress across sessions, reduce effortful or potentially aversive consequences of errors, and support the links where abandonment is most likely.
The relevant consequence may be access to a benefit or avoidance of fines, lost eligibility, or interrupted care.

These distinctions matter because the consequences maintaining behavior, including the termination or avoidance of aversive events, may have different implications for persistence, generalization, countercontrol, and ethical evaluation.
Public-service compliance is thus a useful test case.
It shows why terms like engagement, adherence, or friction reduction are insufficient until translated into functional relations.
A service can be simplified topographically while its consequences remain delayed, errors are followed by aversive events, and competing responses contact more immediate reinforcement.

Conversely, it can support important outcomes when its design specifies the response chain, cuts effort at critical points, arranges effective feedback, and plans for maintenance beyond one-time completion.

Behavior analysis has a strong tradition in behavior-based safety, analyzing accidents and safe conduct as relations among work behavior, conditions, and consequences (Komaki et al., 1978; Sulzer-Azaroff, 1978).

text.text: The same logic extends beyond safety to organizational practices such as reporting, quality checks, knowledge sharing, and procedural adherence.
These are often described as culture, training, or leadership problems but treated here first as contingency problems.
The key questions are functional: what consequences follow the behavior, how immediate they are, what competes with them, and how they are scheduled?
A common failure is reliance on delayed, aggregated outcomes, for example monthly indicators too remote to control daily responses.

Such long-delayed outcomes act indirectly, through rule-governed behavior and verbal histories rather than direct reinforcement (Malott, 1992). Hogan et al. (2009) simulated baggage-screening study makes the point: search behavior rates varied between variable-interval and extinction conditions, consistent with the hypothesis that signal detections may participate in maintaining search responding.

text.text: A second failure is punishing the very behavior the organization claims to value: nearmiss reporting may be encouraged in principle yet immediately followed by paperwork, blame, or surveillance.
Desired responses rarely persist when they seldom contact reinforcement, or contact punishment more reliably than reinforcement (Catania, 2017; Herrnstein, 1970; Sidman, 1989 Sidman, /2000)).

text.text: A behavior-based redesign would not start from "safety culture" or "ethical culture."
It would define the response classes, reduce effort, shield reporting from punitive consequences, acknowledge it immediately, and connect accurate reporting to visible local improvement.

A parallel logic appears in usable security, where usability features may alter effort, stimulus control, and consequences relevant to secure responding (Di Nocera, 2026; Di Nocera & Tempestini, 2022), and in organizational behavior management, where performance feedback is among the field's most common procedures (Balcazar et al., 1989; Prue & Fairbank, 1981).

text.text: Organizational examples also make visible a second level of functional analysis.
The intervention itself must be maintained by someone.
A reporting system may be effective for employees but costly for managers.
A safer procedure may increase response effort or reduce production speed.
A transparent interface may conflict with other organizational outcomes.
Behavior-based design therefore asks not only what maintains the target user's behavior, but what consequences maintain the behavior of those who adopt, implement, modify, and fund the system.
This does not require assuming that organizations have unitary goals.
It requires analyzing the behavior of the relevant actors under their respective contingencies.
This point limits a simple interpretation of behavior-based design as "apply functional analysis at larger scale."
Scale alone is not the issue.
Designed environments involve interdependent contingencies in which the behavior of users, implementers, managers, and designers may be controlled by different consequences.
A functional design account should make these relations explicit when they are relevant to whether the intervention can be implemented or maintained.
When interventions demonstrate immediate effects without assessing maintenance and generalization, it is difficult to determine whether meaningful change has occurred.
In behavior analysis, these outcomes are central rather than optional (Baer et al., 1968; Stokes & Baer, 1977).

text.text: Behavior observed only under engineered prompts has not yet been shown to be durable.
Behavior that fails to transfer may have been trained too narrowly, maintained by artificial consequences, or brought under idiosyncratic stimulus control.
Relapse may be described as lost engagement, reduced motivation, or habit decay.

A functional account asks instead whether reinforcement was artificial and never transferred to natural contingencies, or was thinned too quickly, whether competing behavior continued to be reinforced, whether controlling stimuli disappeared outside the intervention, and whether persistent effort, avoidance, or countercontrol altered performance.
Generalization must be programmed rather than assumed from acquisition in a single setting (Stokes & Baer, 1977).
text.formatted: Generalization must be programmed rather than assumed from acquisition in a single setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Stokes & Baer, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: Differences between training and natural environments may limit generalization, while the absence of effective maintenance contingencies may lead to a decline in responding over time.
Similarly, teaching a single response form does not guarantee that other appropriate responses will occur in new situations.
These are predictable design problems, not mysterious failures of motivation.
For behavior-based design, maintenance and generalization must be considered from the beginning of the design process, not only when evaluating outcomes.
An initial increase in behavior does not necessarily indicate lasting change.
This distinction is particularly important in digital and policy settings, where short-term engagement is often treated as evidence of success.
A click, sign-up, or single attendance may be a useful outcome, but it does not demonstrate that behavior will persist over time.
This distinction also protects behavior-based design from becoming a new label for shortterm behavior change.

A functional specification should state not only how the target response is expected to increase initially, but what will maintain it when prompts, incentives, engineered feedback, or intensive monitoring are withdrawn or altered.
Where no plausible maintenance contingency can be identified, that limitation should be part of the design account rather than discovered only at follow-up.
This perspective also shapes research.

A program in designed environments should treat maintenance, transfer, relapse, and countercontrol as central dependent variables and as part of the phenomenon to be explained, not as complications considered only after an intervention fails.
Aggregate and self-report measures can miss individual variability and within-person patterns such as delayed acquisition or relapse.
An average change can conceal functional heterogeneity when individuals contact different contingencies or change for different reasons.

Behavior analysts can contribute single-case experimental logic where feasible, repeated direct measurement of response classes, and planned replication across contexts and populations (Kazdin, 2020).
text.formatted: Behavior analysts can contribute single-case experimental logic where feasible, repeated direct measurement of response classes, and planned replication across contexts and populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kazdin, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Not every study must become a traditional single-case experiment.
The point is that design research should grow more sensitive to within-person change, repeated contact with contingencies, and the temporal patterns that reveal functional relations.
Behavior-based design places functional specification at the center of the design process.
Whether organizing design around this requirement improves prediction, intervention selection, and behavioral outcomes, however, remains an empirical question.
For example, teams Expertise, design time, and access to information would need to be balanced.
A null result, or a benefit limited to particular problems, would help clarify the conditions under which explicit functional specification provides additional predictive or practical value.

If comparative research consistently fails to identify such benefits, the justification for BBD as a distinct research program would need to be reconsidered, even though functional specification would remain an established component of behavior-analytic practice.
Where formal designs are infeasible, teams can still use repeated measurement, staggered implementation, replication, follow-up probes, and individual-level analysis.
These may not match traditional experimental control, but they strengthen functional inference over one-shot or aggregate pre-post comparisons.
Digital environments already produce fine-grained traces, including clicks, dwell times, errors, latencies, and abandonment points.
The analytic risk is that these traces may be examined without functional hypotheses, explicit contingency mapping, or a distinction between response topography and function.
Behavior analysis can translate them into operant-level variables, consistent with a digital-design logic that breaks behavior into measurable parameters linked to programmed consequences.
The measurement becomes behavior analytic, however, only when events are interpreted in relation to response classes, antecedent control, consequences, histories, and competing contingencies.

This translation requires care: a click is not automatically a response class, dwell time is not direct evidence of engagement, repeated use is not necessarily evidence of reinforcement, and dropout is not necessarily evidence of lost motivation.
A "like" may participate in social approval, status, habit, or a nearly inconsequential interaction, and the same action may enter different contingencies for different users.

Because the same topography can serve different functions and different topographies can serve the same function (Catania, 2017; Cooper et al., 2020), digital traces should be treated as measures that may inform functional hypotheses, rather than as direct evidence of behavioral function.
text.formatted: Because the same topography can serve different functions and different topographies can serve the same function <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Catania, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cooper et al., 2020)</ref>, digital traces should be treated as measures that may inform functional hypotheses, rather than as direct evidence of behavioral function.

text.text: The proposed relations must then be evaluated through appropriate observations and tests.
An important research task for behavior-based design is therefore comparative.
The relevant empirical question is not simply whether behavior analysis can redescribe an existing intervention.
It is whether a functional specification changes what researchers predict, manipulate, measure, or conclude.

Studies that compare interventions selected from the same broad category but based on different functional hypotheses would provide a stronger test of the proposed added value than terminological translation alone.
A further barrier is language.
Core behavior-analytic terms are precise but not always usable in interdisciplinary teams.
The answer is not to abandon precision but to translate in ways that preserve function.
Scientific vocabularies earn their keep by preserving distinctions that matter for prediction and influence.
Terms such as signal, friction, and feedback can facilitate interdisciplinary communication, but their use does not establish the underlying behavioral functions.
A signal may function as a discriminative stimulus, friction may involve response effort, and feedback may acquire different functions depending on the relevant contingencies.
Fogg's Behavior Model shows both the promise and the risk.

Describing behavior as the convergence of motivation, ability, and triggers gives designers an accessible, memorable vocabulary (Fogg, 2009), but one that compresses functionally distinct processes into broad categories.
text.formatted: Describing behavior as the convergence of motivation, ability, and triggers gives designers an accessible, memorable vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fogg, 2009)</ref>, but one that compresses functionally distinct processes into broad categories.

text.text: "Motivation" may mean motivating operations, reinforcement histories, rulegoverned behavior, or social contingencies.
"Ability" or simplicity may mean response effort, skill repertoires, resources, or cognitive load.
"Triggers" may be prompts, discriminative stimuli, or occasions for rule-following.
Fogg's own distinction among sparks, facilitators, and signals partly acknowledges this, yet still keeps different functions under one design label.
The model provides an accessible framework for organizing design decisions, but its categories do not specify the functional relations among antecedent conditions, behavior, and consequences.
These relations must be identified and tested to explain how a particular design influences behavior.
The same need for functional precision applies to other constructs commonly used in behavioral design.
Present bias can be examined in relation to the effects of immediate and delayed consequences (Odum, 2011).
text.formatted: Present bias can be examined in relation to the effects of immediate and delayed consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Odum, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Status quo bias may involve differences in response effort and the contingencies associated with available alternatives (Friman & Poling, 1995).
text.formatted: Status quo bias may involve differences in response effort and the contingencies associated with available alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Friman & Poling, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Social proof may involve imitation and socially mediated consequences (Baer et al., 1967), while engagement may be examined through patterns of repeated responding, reinforcement schedules, and competing contingencies (Ferster & Skinner, 1957; Herrnstein, 1970).
text.formatted: Social proof may involve imitation and socially mediated consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baer et al., 1967)</ref>, while engagement may be examined through patterns of repeated responding, reinforcement schedules, and competing contingencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Ferster & Skinner, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Herrnstein, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: These constructs can be useful for describing behavioral patterns, but their use in design requires identifying the functional relations relevant to each situation.
The aim is not to replace familiar terms with behavior-analytic terminology, but to specify the variables that can be measured and manipulated.
A similar issue arises in recent work on evidence-based digital design.

León Domínguez (2025) applies operant concepts directly, describing digital services as arrangements of discriminative stimuli, measurable responses, programmed consequences, and reinforcement schedules, while also blending in cognitive constructs such as beliefs, expectations, and goaldirected behavior.
It supports the present argument indirectly: behavior-analytic concepts are highly relevant to digital design, but their interdisciplinary use requires careful functional specification.
Some translations are productive when they stay functionally anchored.
Response effort can be discussed in terms of friction, and discriminative stimulus control can be explained through cues that signal when responding is likely to produce particular consequences.
Reinforcement can be described in accessible terms as a process in which consequences increase the future likelihood of responding.
The same discipline should govern translations of generalization, extinction, and competing contingencies.
Handled carefully, such translations let behavior analysts act as design collaborators rather than post hoc critics, and connect the field to design thinking.
Design thinking contributes problem framing and iteration (Brown, 2008; Liedtka, 2015).
text.formatted: Design thinking contributes problem framing and iteration <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Liedtka, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Behavior analysis contributes functional assessment, contingency design, repeated measurement, and maintenance programming.
Together, they can support interventions that are both human-centered and functionally rigorous.
Communicating behavior-analytic contributions to designers and other professional communities will require domain-specific research, examples, and vocabularies.
Interdisciplinary translation should therefore be treated as a continuing research task rather than as something that can be accomplished through a single conceptual article.

The challenge is to avoid two symmetrical errors: jargonistic purity, which preserves technical language but fails to influence practice, and conceptual dilution, which translates terms so loosely that their function disappears.
Behavior-based design needs the middle path: accessible language with rigorous contingency analysis behind it.
The ethical stakes are substantial.
Designed environments do not merely inform.
They arrange contingencies: changing effort, access, delay, and the probability or cost of consequences.

These arrangements can support important outcomes but can also produce compliance, dependency, avoidance, restricted choice, or countercontrol (Sidman, 1989 (Sidman, /2000;; Skinner, 1971; Wolf, 1978).
text.formatted: These arrangements can support important outcomes but can also produce compliance, dependency, avoidance, restricted choice, or countercontrol <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sidman, 1989</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Sidman, /2000;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Skinner, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Wolf, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: The concern is acute in digital environments, where the same elements that increase access or engagement may also sustain patterns of use that mainly benefit the platform.
A behavior-based approach makes these relations explicit.
Whose behavior is being selected, to what ends, and by which consequences?
Are those consequences transparent or hidden?
Are their costs fairly distributed?
Does the design widen meaningful choice or restrict it while calling the result engagement, and does it rely on reinforcement, punishment, or coercion?
These are functional questions as much as ethical ones.
This is why taxonomic labels can be ethically insufficient.
"Engagement," "personalization," or "gamification" may arrange very different contingencies, some expanding access and easing useful behavior, others sustaining use that benefits mainly the designer.
A default may spare needless effort or exploit inaction.
A reminder may help someone reach a delayed benefit or serve as aversive stimulation that maintains compliance.
The organizational level is relevant here as well.
A design cannot be evaluated only by whether it changes a user's behavior.
Contingency transparency also requires examining the consequences that may maintain the behavior of those responsible for designing and implementing the environment.
User welfare, completion, retention, productivity, revenue, compliance, and reduced administrative cost need not align.
Making these contingencies explicit does not determine the ethical answer, but it makes potential conflicts more visible.
Contingency transparency is thus both a scientific and an ethical requirement: interventions should be described by the relations they arrange, not only the outcomes they intend.
It also demands attention to countercontrol.
When people resist, avoid, or disengage, that is not automatically irrationality or low motivation.
It may be a functional response to coercive, opaque, effortful, or poorly reinforced environments.
The next step is to build a cumulative research program, not simply establish a new label.
Behavior-based design will be useful only insofar as it develops and tests functional specifications that offer something beyond behavior-analytic redescription.

Its starting point should be bounded problems in deliberately designed environments, such as repeated errors, abandonment of service procedures, persistence of insecure routines, or allocation among competing responses.
Such problems call for sustained collaborations with designers, engineers, human factors researchers, public administrators, and other domain experts.

The role of behavior analysts is not to displace those specialists but to contribute response-class definitions, explicit hypotheses about relevant contingencies, measures capable of distinguishing alternative interpretations, and plans for maintenance and generalization.
Participating at problem formulation and during design, rather than solely after implementation, may make this contribution more consequential.
A cumulative program also requires empirical accountability.
Studies should determine whether functional specification actually changes predictions, intervention selection, measurement, replication, durability, or ethical appraisal.
Immediate clicks, sign-ups, and shortterm compliance may be legitimate outcomes, but they should not be mistaken for maintenance, generalization, or transfer.
Equally important are the contingencies affecting those who implement and sustain an intervention, and the possibility that nominally beneficial arrangements generate countercontrol or dependency.
Training and disciplinary visibility should grow from such empirical work.
Research partnerships, replications, graduate projects, and domain-specific publications can establish practical exemplars that others can challenge and extend.
The issue is not to defend a label for its own sake, but to make behavior-analytic expertise usable in fields that are already designing environments intended to influence behavior.
If these efforts do not add predictive or practical value, BBD will have little justification as a separate programmatic designation.
Contemporary behavior-change practice has made behavior a central object of design, policy, and implementation.
Its frameworks and taxonomies have improved communication, classification, and reporting, creating conditions under which behavior can be deliberately arranged and evaluated.
The argument of this article is not that contemporary behavioral design generally lacks functional thinking, or that behavior analysis offers principles unknown to other fields.
The narrower claim is that intervention categories and broad explanatory labels do not, by themselves, guarantee functional specification.
Questions remain about response classes, controlling conditions, consequences, competing contingencies, maintenance, generalization, and the behavior of those responsible for the design.
Behavior-based design is therefore not a new theory of behavior or a renamed form of applied behavior analysis.
It is a programmatic use of behavior analysis in deliberately designed environments, organized around functional specification as a design requirement.

Its value will depend on whether this additional specification produces better questions, different predictions, more informative measurement, more durable interventions, clearer analyses of failure, or greater ethical transparency.
A research program must test those claims rather than assume them.

The immediate task is not to persuade every neighboring discipline through one general argument, but to build conceptual and empirical examples that make later interdisciplinary collaboration possible.
Different communities will require different forms of engagement.
The contribution of behavior analysis is to specify relations that can be investigated and tested.

Behavior-based design names that programmatic possibility: behavior analysts working with other professional communities to specify, test, and ethically examine the functional relations embedded in designed environments, while demonstrating rather than assuming the value of doing so.
These obstacles are reasons to organize, not to withdraw.
The problem is not a lack of tools but the opportunity to develop a more visible, cumulative, interdisciplinary program that puts them to work in designed environments.
Building one requires not abandoning behavioranalytic foundations but translating them into research questions, collaborations, methods, and demonstrations legible outside traditional settings.
Such a program need not begin by creating complete training systems or placing behavior analysts in every design domain.

Researchers can start with recurring behavioral problems in one domain, collaborate with professionals already working there, map the functional relations implied by existing interventions, derive competing predictions from alternative specifications, and test whether the additional functional information improves intervention selection, maintenance, generalization, or explanation.

Successful cases can then provide the research questions, collaborations, exemplars, and training opportunities that a larger program would require.A preliminary illustration is provided by Steady State, a physical, two-player educational game in which task allocation, postponement, and resource management were specified through response classes, programmed consequences, competing demands, and repeated in-game measures(Di Nocera & Tinella, 2026).

The pilot provided a preliminary illustration of contingencyinformed design specification, without establishing educational effectiveness.

The other would additionally require explicit functional hypotheses concerning response chains, stimulus control, effort, consequences, and competing contingencies.
